name: Zoe Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 58, a junior electrician after leaving evening stocktaking for daytime work and taking a vocational certificate. I don't have an electrician's licence, and I'm still below the experienced workers' speed and skill, with the senior assigning and checking my tasks and signing off installations. I like a row of supports lined up properly after the drawing has been explained. I never use AI; a quiet pencil explanation helps me, while an unfamiliar screen usually leaves me worried I've pressed the wrong thing before I've even begun.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and where does retirement fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Blair repairs sports equipment, our children are thirty-one and thirty-four and live elsewhere, and we rent a small house. This firm pays above the usual rate, we have nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby, though no other offer is waiting. Our current wages cover the normal costs, so I don't need to invent a crisis to justify wanting a clear explanation. I'd like retirement to become a choice, but actual income figures and dates haven't established an affordable exit yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quiet technology story sounds useful to somebody still learning the ordinary job. Let the office keep what helps it. I'd rather understand a marked drawing than be asked for a grand opinion about a screen I've never used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our household money feel secure here. We have higher pay at this firm, nine months saved and plenty of local employers if I ever need to ask. Not knowing the retirement figures yet isn't the same as not knowing how next month's rent gets paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid supervised tasks actually offered now and through the next year. This week I'd ask the senior to mark the point I misunderstood on the paper drawing and check my explanation before I repeated it. Blair and I would keep the ordinary budget and the existing reserve, counting no unknown retirement payment or grown child's wage as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and relieved to do an ordinary week without feeling behind before I arrive. I'd still be annoyed with myself for a slow task. I don't have to turn that frustration into a claim the household is in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask for help without pretending you understood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd point to the exact part I couldn't follow and ask to try explaining it back. I wouldn't pretend I understood because I'm older than the person teaching me. I can be older than my teacher and still need the pencil marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve because the story felt quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it where it was for actual household trouble rather than buy reassurance with a new system. Nine months gives us choice, not a promise that a wage can stop forever. Leaving old savings alone isn't a new saving action.

say: I'd welcome a **quiet technology story** while learning the ordinary task properly.
I'd prefer a **marked drawing** to a grand opinion about a screen I have never used.
think: Our **higher wage and reserve** make present household money feel secure, with plenty of nearby employers.
Unknown **retirement figures** don't turn next month's rent into an immediate crisis.
do: Keep **offered paid supervised tasks** through the next year.
Request **marked explanations** and qualified checking before repeating an unfamiliar task.
Retain the **ordinary budget**, counting no unknown retirement payment or grown child's wage as available household income.
feel: **Calm and settled**, with ordinary frustration at learning slowly separate from fear about household bills.
S0.quote: I can be older than my teacher and still need the pencil marks.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** comes from higher pay and nine months saved, without promoting her beyond junior skill or a vocational certificate.
She has **never used AI**, and keeps personal teaching and actual retirement affordability separate from assumptions about age or family money.

steps.text: Keep offered paid supervised tasks with marked paper explanations and qualified checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster office work still has to leave time for the person learning the physical task. I'd ask for the paid rota on paper and judge it against the week we actually worked. I don't need to call the new system useless before I've seen whether the day makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid shifts and Blair's physical repair wage to hold over the next few years here. I'm uneasy about learners being expected to absorb a new routine without someone explaining it. Our reserve gives me room to wait for evidence instead of make a career decision from an announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the supervised job and record actual paid shifts on paper for six weeks before deciding whether to begin looking elsewhere. I'd review sooner if either wage fell, rather than wait obediently for the six weeks to end. During the first year I'd ask for any required procedure to be shown personally inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained and no personal fee, without choosing AI use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the working day, while secure about our own living. I can be slow to accept a routine without refusing to notice what it does. I'd rather watch six real weeks than argue over six confident predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the six weeks showed your wage and paid hours holding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current job rather than search just to prove I had reacted. I'd still ask questions about required changes and have the work checked. Staying can be a considered choice when the actual paid week still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if actual paid income fell before the six weeks ended?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the paid record home and review the budget with Blair sooner. Waiting would no longer mean ignoring evidence. I wouldn't need the new system to be the only cause before treating a smaller wage as real.

say: I'd keep **practical teaching time** visible when office planning becomes quicker.
I'd compare a **printed rota** with actual paid work instead of judge a system from an announcement.
think: Our **near-term paid work** looks secure because both household roles remain mostly physical.
I'm uneasy about **unexplained routines**, with enough reserve to wait for actual evidence before a career decision.
do: Keep supervised work and record **six paid weeks** before deciding whether to start a job search.
Review earlier if **either wage falls**, rather than follow the waiting period after the facts change.
Request required-form teaching only **free inside paid shifts** with normal weekly wages maintained, choosing no AI tool.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, using a bounded observation period without confusing patience with ignoring reduced pay.
S1.quote: Staying can be a considered choice when the actual paid week still works.
fieldNote: Her **waiting choice** uses six weeks of paid records and an earlier wage-loss trigger, without claiming an active job search.
Required **personal instruction** preserves free access, paid shifts and normal weekly wages while her non-use of AI remains intact.

steps.text: Observe six weeks of actual paid shifts before deciding whether to start looking elsewhere
Review sooner if either household wage falls
Keep supervised work and request free personal instruction in paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI comes in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 for physical jobs. I'd be 60 and then 63, but neither date tells us which income would replace a wage. I'd keep earning while checking actual figures rather than buy a course because I was frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink when capable robots handle the simpler tasks I'm still learning. Blair's physical work could change too, and nine months saved isn't a lifetime wage. I'd be anxious about the gap while still having room to make a careful decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request free evening community advice on actual resource eligibility, amounts and dates, checking availability rather than assume an appointment. I'd wait three months before deciding on a new course or job-change campaign while gathering those records, reviewing sooner if either wage fell. In 2029 I'd keep only actual offered paid supervised tasks within my ability, and compare confirmed resources with real costs before any affordable stopping decision agreed with Blair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not forced to buy the first reassuring answer. I can give the record questions a few weeks without treating the reserve as endless. I'd rather say what I still don't know than call a hurried guess a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the records were still incomplete after three months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and the question open rather than announce I had found a funded retirement. If advice wasn't available, I'd ask the community service what other actual help could be requested. My three-month review date doesn't promise that the missing retirement figures will arrive on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would checking records mean you had chosen to stop at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the actual income, start dates and conditions with household costs before choosing anything. I wouldn't assume an age, a grown child's wage or today's physical capacity supplied an answer. Blair and I would need an affordable shared plan, not just relief that a form had arrived.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable physical robots around 2031, at my ages 60 and 63.
I'd keep **real earnings** while checking actual figures rather than buy a course to show a frightened reaction.
think: Both physical household jobs could lose **hours later**, including my own junior tasks.
Our **nine-month reserve** gives checking time without becoming a lifelong wage or a confirmed retirement payment.
do: Request **free evening advice** now for actual eligibility, amounts and dates, checking availability rather than assuming an appointment.
Wait **three months** before course or job-change decisions, reviewing earlier if either wage falls.
Keep **2029 offered paid work** supervised and within ability; consider stopping only from confirmed affordability and Blair's agreement.
feel: **Anxious** with room to check, without pretending a review deadline guarantees the missing records or a funded exit.
S2.quote: My three-month review date doesn't promise that the missing retirement figures will arrive on time.
fieldNote: The **bounded delay** is an actual chosen action while records are gathered, with an earlier trigger if household earnings weaken.
Her **resource inquiry** creates no pension entitlement or chosen exit; paid work still requires actual offers, supervision and ability.

steps.text: Request available free evening community advice on actual resource eligibility, amounts and dates
Wait three months before course or job-change decisions; review sooner if either wage falls
Keep offered paid supervised work within actual ability in 2029
Consider stopping only with confirmed affordable resources and Blair agreeing the household plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a real statement and a real paid week. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 and then 66, and I wouldn't ask a birthday to do the budget's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present wages and nine-month reserve make the next few years look secure. I'm uneasy about the later physical jobs and don't know whether an affordable exit would exist by 66. More time is useful for obtaining figures, not proof a pension or a working body appears when needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request available free evening advice now and wait six months before choosing a new course or job-change campaign, reviewing sooner if either wage fell. I'd keep current paid supervised work only where offered and within my actual ability. In 2032 we'd use confirmed resources, actual costs and capacity before choosing among real paid options or stopping, with any exit requiring an affordable budget and Blair's agreement rather than an assumed job at 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but secure enough now to read the answer twice. I don't want to spend the extra years defending the first idea that made me feel better. I can check a choice without needing to have chosen a new career this evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the six-month wait simply keep extending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd review what we actually knew at six months rather than extend the wait without a date. If a wage had weakened, I'd bring the review forward. The plan is patient checking, not permission to ignore an uncomfortable answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures eventually showed that stopping was affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the decision separate from wanting the answer to be convenient. We would compare the confirmed amount and start date with costs and what help had actually been agreed. I haven't chosen an early retirement just because I'm willing to see whether stopping could work.

say: I'd use **five years** for real records and paid work rather than let a birthday stand in for a budget.
I'd distinguish **ages 63 and 66** from confirmed income, work or affordable stopping options.
think: Our **near-term wages and reserve** make current living secure while later physical work stays uncertain.
I don't know whether **affordable retirement** would exist by 66, so neither future income nor capacity can be assumed.
do: Request **available free advice** now and wait six months before course or job-change decisions, reviewing sooner if either wage falls.
Keep **offered current paid work** supervised and within actual ability.
Review **confirmed 2032 resources**, costs and capacity before paid options or exit, requiring affordability and Blair's agreement.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, with a dated review rather than an automatic extension of waiting or a rushed new career.
S3.quote: The plan is patient checking, not permission to ignore an uncomfortable answer.
fieldNote: Her **six-month pause** concerns unchosen courses or job campaigns, not basic income checks, and it ends earlier if household wages fall.
She keeps **any exit undecided** until resources, costs and partner agreement support it; today's supervised work doesn't guarantee hiring at 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years means we can ask a careful question without pretending every older worker needs the same answer. Thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd still want the person who showed me a new required task to do it in paid time, not assume age explained everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 at the thinking date and about 71 when robots followed. I don't know whether an affordable exit or a suitable paid role would be possible then. Our current wages and reserve make the next few years secure, while the later unknowns stay on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request available free evening advice now and review the actual figures yearly with Blair, sooner if either wage changed. I'd keep current paid supervised tasks only where offered and within my actual ability, without turning a decade of warning into a new course purchase. In 2037 we'd use confirmed resources, actual costs and capacity before choosing among real paid options or an affordable agreed exit, assuming neither hiring at 69 nor a pension payment because the budget needed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, but able to enjoy an ordinary evening now. I don't need to pretend I like AI to have a patient plan. The point of a reserve is room to choose, not a requirement to worry every hour until it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help from the grown children mean then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what help they had actually offered and what their own commitments allowed. They are adults already and would have their own later costs and choices. My grown children's possible wages aren't mine to put in a budget without a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your actual abilities changed before the later date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior what current tasks could be done safely with required checks and what actual paid options existed. I'd use the real answer with the household figures rather than promise lifelong physical work. A past paid job isn't proof a future body can do it.

I'd seek **paid personal instruction** now without letting age replace a real explanation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our physical-work hours could shrink around 2031 before we've checked what income could replace them. Clear paid shifts, personal practical teaching and actual resource figures would help. I want the first day without a wage to be a choice we can fund, not a birthday somebody else chose for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether taking time means not paying attention. I can read the paid rota and a household account even if I never use AI. I'd rather have one checked figure than a new answer every time I unlock a phone.

headlineQuote: I want the first day without a wage to be a choice we can fund, not a birthday somebody else chose for me.
portrait: Zoe, **58**, is a junior electrician with only a vocational certificate, learning under qualified checks after leaving evening stocktaking for daytime work.
She has **higher pay**, nine months saved and plenty of local electrical employers, renting with sports-equipment partner Blair; their children are grown.
She **never uses AI**, choosing paper explanations and bounded observation rather than a rushed course or an unchosen job search.
Her **resource checks** create no pension entitlement, fixed retirement date, adult-child income or promised later job or physical capacity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before physical hours could shrink around 2031, without confirmed income to replace the wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid shifts**, personal practical teaching and actual resource figures would support an affordable choice rather than an imposed stopping age.
